title: Map reachable services without assuming vulnerability
scope: Authorized external unauthenticated, internal network, and local administrator views; report each separately. Start with configuration and a small approved port list, not a network-wide scan.
concepts: A listening service, a reachable port, and an exploitable service are different facts. A TCP connection establishes reachability from one source at one time. A port label is usually a convention, not proof of the application or its version. Firewalls, NAT, load balancers, IPv6, and split DNS can make external and internal observations differ.

Build a service register containing asset owner, intended clients, listener address, transport, business purpose, expected authentication, and management plane. Compare observed exposure with that register. An unexpected administrator interface is an exposure finding even without a demonstrated exploit. A filtered or silent result is inconclusive about the service behind the boundary.

discover.title: One approved TCP port from a recorded vantage
discover.code:
# Windows PowerShell; obtain written approval and replace the documentation host.
# One TCP connection attempt, not application identification.
Test-NetConnection -ComputerName service.example.invalid -Port 443 -InformationLevel Detailed
discover.interpretation: Record source address, destination address, port, time, and TcpTestSucceeded. True means a connection worked from this source; false can mean filtering, routing failure, unavailable host, or no listener. Do not extrapolate to UDP or other sources.

discover.title: Local listener inventory
discover.code:
# Authorized Windows host session; process attribution may need elevated read access.
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Select-Object LocalAddress,LocalPort,OwningProcess
Get-NetUDPEndpoint | Select-Object LocalAddress,LocalPort,OwningProcess
discover.interpretation: Join process IDs to the approved process/service inventory. Wildcard bindings include multiple interfaces; loopback bindings are normally local-only. Local listeners do not prove remote reachability, and process IDs can change.

verify: Agree asset addresses, source networks, approved ports, rate, window, owner contact, and stop conditions. Fragile appliances require owner review before even basic connections. Stop if error rates or service latency rise.
Export current firewall, listener, ingress, DNS, and load-balancer configuration. Record IPv4 and IPv6 destinations and whether a proxy answers instead of the origin.
Attempt only the approved connection checks from each approved vantage; record exact outcomes. For application identity use owner configuration and deployed inventory, not the port number alone.
For every unexpected reachable endpoint, document intended versus actual clients and whether authentication is required. Gather configuration evidence of sensitive functions without invoking them.

branches.condition: Reachable from an unauthorized network
branches.outcome: Confirm the destination and route with the owner; report excessive exposure, not a CVE.

branches.condition: Internal connection succeeds but external check fails
branches.outcome: Record an internal attack surface and a boundary observation; do not describe the service as absent.

branches.condition: No response or incomplete asset inventory
branches.outcome: Mark coverage incomplete and reconcile routing and owner evidence before closing.

fix: Remove unused listeners and ingress rules through change control.
Restrict management planes to approved administration networks and identities. Bind local-only services to loopback; review IPv6 separately.
Assign each remaining service an owner, support lifecycle, authentication policy, and exposure baseline.
retest: Repeat the same port checks from the same source networks and address families; retain before/after records.
Confirm expected clients still connect and unintended clients cannot. Reconcile host listeners with edge rules; closure of one route does not establish closure of all routes.
detection: Alert on new listeners or ingress rules outside the baseline and retain actor/change-ticket context.
Correlate rejected connections and unexpected management access with destination ownership. An absence of firewall logs is not proof that no traffic arrived.

provenance.reason: Separates internal hosts from systems visible to outsiders and calls for documenting accessible hosts.
Explains packet/response scanning and that OS identification is a guess.
Warns that scanning can produce false positives and denial of service; motivates bounded owner-approved checks.

title: Establish vulnerability applicability and effective patch state
scope: Read-only asset, package, and vendor-advisory assessment. Remote banners are leads; authenticated administrator evidence is a separate vantage. No exploit validation.
concepts: A vulnerability claim needs a specific product/component, vendor-defined affected conditions, and evidence that those conditions apply to the deployed asset. A generic scanner result, error, or open port cannot prove a CVE. Preserve advisory identity, retrieval date, affected/fixed ranges, required configuration, and the asset evidence used to decide applicability.

Installed and running versions can differ after an update. Packages may contain backported fixes without matching an upstream version string. Containers, bundled libraries, appliances, and alternate installations need their own evidence. Scheduled update cycles help planning but urgent out-of-band fixes still need a response process.

discover.title: Windows update clues
discover.code:
# Authorized local Windows read access; this is not a complete update inventory.
Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem | Select-Object Caption,Version,BuildNumber,LastBootUpTime
Get-HotFix | Select-Object HotFixID,InstalledOn
discover.interpretation: Use the build and listed updates as evidence to reconcile with the vendor's servicing guidance and management platform. Get-HotFix omits some update types and application patches. Empty output, a recent install date, or a listed KB does not establish that all affected components are fixed.

verify: Collect product edition, platform, architecture, package/build identifiers, installation source, running binary identity, and relevant feature configuration. Record collection method and privileges.

Use current vendor advisories to make a per-asset applicability table: affected, fixed, not affected with reason, or unknown. Check distribution backport notices and superseding cumulative updates rather than assuming an upstream string is authoritative.

Reconcile scanner findings against this table. Separate a confirmed affected version/configuration from an unverified heuristic and from demonstrated exploitation; this guide establishes only the first two.
Verify deployment completion, required service restarts or reboots, and the running component after maintenance. Track unreachable assets and exceptions with owners and dates.

branches.condition: Vendor conditions match and effective fix is absent
branches.outcome: Record confirmed applicability, reachable interfaces, and impact from the advisory; prioritize by exposure and business consequence.

branches.condition: Version looks old but vendor documents a backport
branches.outcome: Retain package revision and vendor notice; do not override documented servicing evidence with a banner.

branches.condition: Component identity or advisory conditions cannot be established
branches.outcome: Keep the finding unverified and request inventory evidence; do not invent affected versions.

fix: Deploy supported vendor fixes using the approved maintenance process; test application compatibility and dependencies.
If no fix is available, use vendor-supported feature restrictions or access controls and record residual risk, owner, and expiry. Isolation is mitigation, not patch installation.
Replace unsupported components and verify that old deployable artifacts cannot silently reintroduce them.
retest: Recollect installed and running identifiers after required maintenance and compare with the exact advisory conditions.
Repeat only safe inventory/scanner checks approved for the asset; document discrepancies and test business functionality.
Close only assets with effective fix evidence; keep failed deployments and inaccessible systems visible.
detection: Monitor failed deployments, overdue exceptions, and reappearance of affected package revisions.
Use vulnerability-specific indicators only when supported by vendor guidance; generic connection or error events are not evidence of CVE exploitation.

provenance.reason: Discusses vendor patch processes, cumulative updates, and out-of-band resource constraints.
Explains that patch interpretation depends on disclosed information; motivates evidence-based applicability rather than assuming every code difference is a security fix.

title: Trace web input into database and process boundaries
scope: Authorized source/configuration review and benign functional checks on approved application routes. Distinguish anonymous inputs from authenticated user and administrator inputs.
concepts: Injection occurs when data becomes part of an interpreter's instructions. SQL string concatenation and shell command construction are different sinks with the same boundary failure. A logged-in user remains an untrusted input source; authentication before a dangerous operation does not make submitted data safe.

Input validation expresses allowed types, lengths, ranges, and business values. It does not replace parameter binding or safe process APIs. Encoding conversion after validation can change the meaning of a character, so review decoding, normalization, validation, and sink use as a complete sequence. Error-free ordinary requests do not establish injection resistance.
verify: List entry points including query fields, JSON, headers, imported files, background jobs, and authenticated forms. Record required role and which application component receives each input.

Trace representative fields through decoding and validation to database calls, shell/process APIs, templates, and stored procedures. Gather redacted code excerpts with revision and call path; do not collect user secrets.

For SQL verify actual parameter binding, including inside stored procedures; dynamic table/column names need explicit allowlisted mappings. For process execution verify a fixed executable and separate argument array with no shell and no attacker-controlled options.

On approved non-production routes submit ordinary text, a documented valid boundary value, and a mildly out-of-range plain value within a small agreed size. Confirm documented validation behavior using request IDs and application logs; do not submit interpreter syntax or execution requests.
Record whether rejection happens server-side before sink use. A validation error proves only that particular input was rejected; source/trace evidence is needed for the broader conclusion.

branches.condition: Untrusted input is concatenated into interpreted SQL or a shell command
branches.outcome: Report the unsafe data-to-code path and its reachable role; do not need or create an exploit payload.

branches.condition: Validation is client-only or precedes meaning-changing conversion
branches.outcome: Treat the server boundary as unverified until validation is enforced on the representation actually used.

branches.condition: Only black-box benign requests are available
branches.outcome: Report observed behavior and coverage limits, not an injection-free assurance.

fix: Use database parameter APIs for values and allowlisted identifiers; eliminate dynamic SQL where possible.
Replace shell invocation with library operations or fixed process/argument APIs; validate option values and restrict service account privileges.
Define one decoding/normalization policy and validate the final representation server-side. Use bounded error responses without query text, paths, or secrets.
retest: Review the changed source path to confirm all inputs reach safe sinks; test valid business values and documented invalid boundaries.
Check alternate routes, stored procedures, and background consumers. Confirm database/process permissions are limited and legitimate work still succeeds.
detection: Correlate validation failures, database exceptions, and unexpected child processes with request IDs and roles.
Retain error categories rather than raw sensitive input. Establish a normal failure baseline and investigate changes without treating every syntax error as exploitation.

provenance.reason: Shows that password authentication before shell construction does not protect a controllable command argument.
Explains SQL query construction from untrusted network strings.
Describes verification in one encoding followed by security-sensitive use in another.

title: Assess browser rendering and DOM trust boundaries
scope: Approved web pages, source review, and inert marker checks. Separate immediate reflection, stored rendering, and client-side DOM flows; do not execute injected code.
concepts: Browser injection is a rendering-boundary problem: an untrusted value is interpreted as markup or code rather than displayed as data. The relevant context can be HTML text, an attribute, a URL, script, or a DOM API. One escaping function is not correct for all contexts.

Reflected data returns in the current response; stored data is rendered later, possibly to a privileged viewer; DOM data can come from URL state or client storage without appearing in the server response. Finding a plain marker establishes data flow, not script execution. Browser filtering and security headers are supplementary controls, not substitutes for correcting an unsafe sink.
verify: Map user-controllable fields and later viewers, including administration screens and reports. Use synthetic records only and get approval before any persistent test data.
Submit a unique inert alphanumeric marker such as ASSESSMENTMARKER2026 through normal allowed UI behavior. Record route, role, request ID, response content type, and all places the marker appears.

Inspect response source and the final DOM with browser developer tools. Identify whether the marker becomes a text node, attribute, URL, or markup, and distinguish server output from client-side transformations.

Review source-to-sink paths for unsafe HTML insertion, script construction, and URL scheme handling. Confirm framework autoescaping remains enabled and that trusted-HTML exceptions cannot receive ordinary user input.
Review cookie protections and content security policy as defense in depth. A marker displayed correctly or a strict policy does not prove that every rendering path is safe.

branches.condition: User data reaches an HTML/code sink without context-appropriate handling
branches.outcome: Document the code path and affected viewers as an unsafe rendering finding; do not run a script demonstration.

branches.condition: Marker is plain text but source coverage is incomplete
branches.outcome: Record the tested path as behaving correctly; retain uncertainty for other contexts and roles.

branches.condition: Client code alone handles rendering
branches.outcome: Assess DOM sinks independently of server-response escaping.

fix: Prefer text-node APIs and framework escaping. Use context-appropriate encoding at output; avoid constructing script from data.
For intentional rich text use a maintained allowlist sanitizer and constrain URL schemes; document trusted-HTML boundaries.
Apply a supported restrictive content security policy and secure session cookies without treating them as the primary fix.
retest: Repeat inert marker flows in immediate, stored, and administrative views; inspect DOM and source after the change.
Review every changed sink and test permitted rich text and URLs for correct business behavior. Remove approved synthetic records via normal application controls.
detection: Monitor rendering exceptions and policy violation reports with route and release identifiers; strip sensitive content from reports.
Correlate unusual saved-content changes with viewer errors and audit events. Policy reports alone do not establish a successful attack.

provenance.reason: Defines XSS as changed browser behavior and explains impact beyond a demonstration dialog.
Explicitly says to fix known XSS rather than rely on browser protection, and discusses client-side validation limitations.

title: Verify identity, sessions, and object-level authorization
scope: Owner-provisioned synthetic users with documented roles and test objects. No guessing credentials, enumeration of real users, lockout testing, or credential attacks.
concepts: Authentication identifies a principal; authorization decides whether that principal may perform an action on a particular object. A successful login does not justify access to another tenant's records or administrator functions. Hidden UI controls are not server-side authorization.

Session validity must follow the application's policy for expiry, logout, privilege changes, and revocation. Test transport, identity provider, application, and background access separately where applicable. Database grants and application roles are separate layers; an overprivileged database identity can expand the impact of an application defect.
verify: Obtain an anonymous context and synthetic accounts for two ordinary users, a separate tenant if applicable, and an administrator. Create a role/action/object matrix with expected allow and deny decisions; the owner must approve this matrix.
Use normal login with supplied credentials and inspect session cookie attributes and documented expiry/revocation configuration. Keep tokens and passwords out of evidence.

For read-only approved endpoints compare own-object access, the explicitly provided other test object's identifier, and administrator-only access. Record status, redacted body, role, request ID, and server decision. Do not discover identifiers or access real user data.

Distinguish an actual denial from a login redirect or an error page returning sensitive data. For actions that change state, use code/policy review or separately approved synthetic functional tests rather than issuing speculative requests.

Perform one normal logout with a test session and verify the protected read is denied afterward under the documented revocation policy. Review password/MFA/reset configuration without probing guesses or recovery tokens.

branches.condition: A test user receives another test principal's protected data or privileged function
branches.outcome: Report the exact role/object boundary failure and redact data; stop before expanding access.

branches.condition: UI blocks access but server decisions are not checked
branches.outcome: Authorization remains unverified.

branches.condition: A logged-out session remains valid contrary to policy
branches.outcome: Document a session revocation defect, including timing and expected policy; do not infer credential compromise.

fix: Enforce deny-by-default authorization on every server action using authenticated principal, object ownership/tenant, and permitted operation.
Centralize session lifecycle and revocation policy, secure cookies and transport, and protect high-risk actions with appropriate reauthentication/MFA.
Minimize application database grants and review recovery and service-account policies independently of UI roles.
retest: Repeat every allow and deny cell using fresh synthetic sessions and the same test objects, including anonymous access.
Confirm authorized users still work and logout/role-change decisions follow policy. Check logs without exposing tokens.
detection: Log authorization decisions with principal identifier, object category, action, and request ID, avoiding sensitive record contents.
Investigate repeated denied cross-tenant actions and privilege changes; validate alerts with a single approved synthetic deny event, not credential attacks.

provenance.reason: Separates authentication, authorization, confidentiality, integrity, and availability in protocol security.
Shows how to inspect assigned database privileges rather than assume role names imply restrictions.
Explains that connection privileges and powerful file privileges have distinct consequences.

title: Assess file access, canonicalization, and upload boundaries
scope: Source and permission review plus owner-created benign file fixtures. Distinguish remote application access, authenticated uploads, and local service-account access. No attempts to read operating-system secrets.
concepts: A user-visible name is not a safe filesystem authority. Decoding, separator handling, case rules, Unicode conversion, archive extraction, and symbolic links can change the object a path denotes. Validate the representation actually used and enforce containment using filesystem-aware operations, not a simple string-prefix comparison.

File risk also depends on the account performing the operation and where uploaded bytes are stored. A database FILE privilege or a broadly privileged service account can expose host files even when the remote user has no direct filesystem login. An upload should be treated as untrusted data, not executable application content. Path review here is a defensive synthesis of the books' encoding and file-privilege lessons, not a reproduced traversal lab.
verify: Inventory download, upload, import, export, archive, template, and logging paths. Record who can choose names and how application identifiers map to actual files.

Trace decoding and normalization through the final open/create operation. Review containment checks, path-component rules, link handling, race protection, and behavior for existing versus new files. Retain code revision and approved root configuration.

Ask the owner to provision harmless files inside the approved root and in a separate test-only root. Verify ordinary allowed access through the application; verify rejection of disallowed locations through reviewed automated tests or policy evidence, without transmitting traversal strings or reading real host files.

Review effective service-account permissions and database grants. Establish whether the account can read or write outside its needed roots; permission evidence is sufficient, so do not demonstrate access to sensitive files.

For uploads inspect size/count limits, server-selected names, content policy, non-executable storage, authorization for retrieval, and archive extraction containment. Use only small approved text fixtures and normal names.

branches.condition: User-selected paths can reach an unrestricted filesystem operation
branches.outcome: Document missing containment and service-account impact without accessing outside data.

branches.condition: Checks occur before a meaning-changing conversion or link resolution
branches.outcome: Containment is not established; request filesystem-aware implementation evidence.

branches.condition: Uploads are outside the web root but a processor still executes them
branches.outcome: Assess the downstream processing boundary; storage location alone is not a complete control.

fix: Map opaque application IDs to server-controlled files and restrict operations to explicit roots with component-aware containment and safe link/race handling.
Store uploads under generated names in non-executable storage; enforce bounded sizes, approved types, authorization, and safe archive processing.
Remove unnecessary host and database file privileges; separate read, write, and processing accounts where practical.
retest: Repeat approved fixture operations and reviewed negative containment tests; verify allowed files still work and denied locations remain inaccessible.
Recheck permissions, upload handlers, and archive/link behavior after deployment. Remove benign fixtures through approved application/owner procedures.
detection: Log denied file operations using stable object IDs and reason categories rather than sensitive absolute paths or contents.
Monitor writes to application executable/configuration directories and changes in file privileges; correlate with application identity and deployment activity.

provenance.reason: Explicitly identifies security checks in one encoding followed by resource access using another as a dangerous sequence.
Explains that database FILE privilege can read files available to the database service user; used for permission-based assessment, not file extraction.

title: Assess parser limits and memory-safety evidence
scope: Developer-assisted code/build review and resource-bounded offline tests on an approved test instance. Production fuzzing and crash triggering are outside this guide.
concepts: A parser must check declared lengths, available bytes, nesting, counts, and arithmetic before allocation or copying. A multiplication or conversion that wraps can allocate less storage than subsequent operations assume. Memory-safe languages reduce some corruption risks but do not automatically prevent resource exhaustion or unsafe native-extension defects.

A crash is evidence of a failure, not proof of remote code execution or a named CVE. To diagnose it preserve the input, build identity, exception/stack, test conditions, and reproducibility. Mutation testing changes existing samples; grammar-based testing follows a format model. Both need bounded budgets and coverage analysis; neither a quiet run nor enabled mitigations proves absence of defects.
verify: List parser entry points, reachable roles, supported formats, maximum document sizes, native libraries, and build identifiers. Prioritize externally supplied content but preserve local-only and authenticated boundaries.

Review count-times-element-size calculations, signed/unsigned conversions, bounds checks, format-string APIs, recursion, decompression limits, and failure cleanup. Check declared lengths against both available bytes and application policy.

Have developers run existing format conformance and boundary tests offline with current compiler/runtime diagnostics appropriate to the stack. Agree CPU, memory, input-count, and time limits; do not adapt a book's live network random-data command.

If a bounded test fails, stop that case and preserve a hash of the synthetic input, stack/diagnostic, exact build, resource usage, and relevant code path. Group repeated failures by root cause; keep dumps private because they may contain secrets.
Assess supported compiler hardening and platform mitigations from build/runtime evidence. Mark uninstrumented or untested components as coverage gaps.

branches.condition: Diagnostic identifies an out-of-bounds operation or arithmetic overflow
branches.outcome: Report the reproducible safety defect and reachable input boundary, not weaponization or assumed exploitability.

branches.condition: Only a timeout or memory spike is observed
branches.outcome: Investigate resource limits and complexity; do not classify it automatically as memory corruption.

branches.condition: No failures but limited corpus or coverage
branches.outcome: Record the tests and limits; absence of observed crashes is not proof of parser safety.

fix: Use checked arithmetic, explicit length validation, bounded allocation, fixed format strings, and safe ownership/lifetime patterns before data access.
Prefer maintained memory-safe parsers where feasible and patch native dependencies. Apply current supported hardening rather than historical protection packages from the labs.
Enforce document, expansion, recursion, concurrency, and execution-time limits; return controlled errors and add regression cases for diagnosed failures.
retest: Run the diagnosed cases and valid corpus against the fixed build offline under the same resource budgets and diagnostics.
Confirm invalid inputs reject cleanly, valid inputs still parse, and regression tests cover the actual root cause. Record changed coverage and residual untested interfaces.
detection: Monitor parser exceptions, repeated process restarts, memory growth, and input rejection categories by component/build.
Restrict crash artifacts and correlate failures with input origin; avoid retaining customer documents unless incident handling explicitly authorizes it.

provenance.reason: Explains wrapped allocation arithmetic producing smaller-than-expected buffers.
Distinguishes mutation and grammar-based testing.
Lists reproducible samples and crash context and explains clustering duplicate crashes.
Warns about live critical systems; unsafe random network fuzzing is deliberately not reused.

title: Review host trust, service identities, and excessive privileges
scope: Authorized local configuration review. Separate what a standard local user can observe from administrator-only evidence; do not execute privilege escalation techniques.
concepts: A privilege problem is often a trust relationship: a powerful process reads a binary, configuration, script, library, or scheduled-task definition that a less privileged principal can modify. Assess both the execution identity and the writers of every trusted artifact and parent directory. Administrator-only read evidence does not demonstrate that an ordinary user can exploit that relationship.

Service accounts need only their documented functions. Broad database grants, filesystem permissions, interactive login, and unrestricted management access can enlarge a defect's impact. Permission names and default configurations vary across platforms and versions; evaluate current effective rights rather than copying historical setup examples.

discover.title: Windows service identity and executable inventory
discover.code:
# Authorized local Windows session; some fields may require elevated read access.
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name,State,StartName,PathName
discover.interpretation: Identify privileged identities and owner-approved executable/configuration locations. Do not execute PathName. Inspect quoted arguments and effective ACLs separately; a privileged identity or unusual path alone does not prove escalation.

discover.title: Review an approved artifact ACL
discover.code:
# Replace with the exact owner-approved path on this host. Read-only ACL display.
Get-Acl -LiteralPath 'C:\ApprovedAssessment\service-config.example' | Format-List Owner,AccessToString
discover.interpretation: Compare writers with the service's trust boundary, including parent-directory rights and inherited groups. ACL display does not calculate all effective access or establish which process consumes this file.

verify: Record platform/build, service owners, administrator groups, service identities, scheduled jobs, and remote management listeners using authorized read access.

For each privileged service identify its binary, scripts, configuration, load/search directories, and update source. Review effective writers and ownership, including inherited directory permissions and group membership.

Review least-privilege requirements, interactive logon rights, credential storage policy, and database grants using redacted configuration. Do not dump credentials or modify service files to demonstrate impact.

Validate suspicious permissions with the owner and platform access-evaluation tools. Establish whether a lower-privilege role has actual write authority and whether a privileged process trusts the artifact; record each fact separately.

branches.condition: Lower-privilege writers control an artifact trusted by a privileged service
branches.outcome: Report the trust/permission defect and code/configuration evidence; no elevation attempt is needed.

branches.condition: Service is privileged but artifacts are protected
branches.outcome: Assess whether privilege is necessary; high privilege alone does not establish a writable-path weakness.

branches.condition: Review was administrator-only
branches.outcome: Label configuration evidence as privileged visibility, not unauthenticated or ordinary-user access.

fix: Run services with narrowly scoped identities; remove unneeded interactive/admin/database privileges.
Protect executable, configuration, script, and search directories against unauthorized writers; use explicit supported paths and controlled deployment permissions.
Restrict management interfaces and manage secrets through supported protected stores. Document exceptions and service dependencies before changing rights.
retest: Recalculate effective rights for the same lower-privilege roles and verify that protected artifacts cannot be modified.
Verify service startup, maintenance, and business operations still function; repeat listener/identity inventory and compare with the approved baseline.
detection: Monitor administrator/group membership changes, service identity/path changes, and writes to protected service artifacts.
Correlate unexpected privileged child processes with service and change records; retain actor and artifact hashes rather than secret contents.

provenance.reason: Demonstrates inspection of assigned grants and powerful grant options.
States that users should not receive unneeded privileges and illustrates the service user's host-file reach.

title: Reconcile dependencies with the code actually running
scope: Authorized build manifests, deployment artifacts, runtime inventories, and supplier advisories. No dependency installation, package-script execution, or vulnerability payloads.
concepts: Applications inherit risk from frameworks, parsers, plugins, runtimes, native libraries, and container base images. A top-level manifest is not the entire dependency graph. Lockfiles describe a resolved build intent; an artifact inventory or SBOM describes shipped components; running-process evidence establishes what is actually loaded. Reconcile all three rather than assuming they agree.

A framework vulnerability is not proven by a recognizable page or a dependency name. Match exact supplier identity, package revision, deployment context, and vendor advisory conditions. Reachability can prioritize work but an unused-looking code path is not a permanent guarantee because configuration and application routes change.

discover.title: Inspect an existing Python environment without installing packages
discover.code:
# Authorized environment; use the owner's exact deployed interpreter.
# Placeholder must be replaced. Does not install or update packages.
<approved-python-interpreter> -m pip list --format=json
discover.interpretation: Capture interpreter identity and environment alongside output. This lists installed distributions, not necessarily imported modules, OS libraries, vendored code, or other environments. Command failure means inventory is incomplete, not dependency absence.

verify: Collect source revision, manifests/lockfiles, artifact hash or image digest, SBOM if available, interpreter/runtime identifiers, and deployment location. Use existing build outputs without resolving/installing untrusted dependencies.

Compare direct and transitive packages with shipped archives, bundled copies, native extensions, plugins, and runtime-loaded components. Include workers and alternate deployments, not only the front-end process.

Map unsupported or potentially affected components to current supplier advisories. Record fixed ranges and distribution backports exactly as documented; classify uncertain identity or applicability as unknown.

Identify supplier/source controls, version pinning, update ownership, and supported lifecycle. Check whether an old artifact can be redeployed and whether the updated runtime actually replaced the loaded old component.

branches.condition: Lockfile and deployed artifact differ
branches.outcome: Use deployed evidence for exposure and investigate build/deployment drift.

branches.condition: A vulnerable framework is installed but feature use is unclear
branches.outcome: Record applicability uncertainty and obtain configuration/call-path evidence; do not probe with an exploit.

branches.condition: No dependency manager inventory is available
branches.outcome: Request supplier artifact/SBOM and runtime evidence; do not report an empty dependency graph.

fix: Upgrade or replace unsupported/affected dependencies following supplier guidance; rebuild and redeploy immutable reviewed artifacts.
Pin reviewed sources and resolutions, retain artifact identity, and prevent unapproved registry/source overrides.
Assign update ownership and remove unnecessary plugins or bundled copies; verify compatibility and restart loaded components as required.
retest: Compare the new artifact and running inventories against the resolved dependency graph and supplier fixed conditions.
Check worker processes and replicas, functional compatibility, and deployment controls that prevent old artifacts returning. Keep unresolved supplier evidence visible.
detection: Alert on manifest/lockfile changes without reviewed build provenance, unexpected package sources, and runtime/artifact drift.
Monitor supplier advisories and lifecycle changes for the recorded inventory; keep notification routing tied to component owners.

provenance.reason: Explains framework-provided functionality and high-impact Struts vulnerabilities; the historical exploit environment is not reused.
Motivates ongoing supplier-specific update handling including urgent releases.

title: Assess network and VoIP signaling, media, and management exposure
scope: Owner configuration review, approved reachability observations, and consented synthetic calls. Distinguish Internet, user LAN, voice LAN, and management views. No interception of real calls, registration attacks, or call disruption.
concepts: VoIP has separate signaling, media, and management paths. Signaling authentication does not establish media confidentiality. TLS protecting SIP on one hop does not automatically protect other hops or the RTP media stream. Review each endpoint, proxy, gateway, and recording leg; a protected handset leg can coexist with an unprotected downstream leg.

Media protection needs negotiated encryption and integrity, validated peers, and an appropriate key-management policy. SRTP packets resemble RTP, so a port or packet appearance alone cannot establish negotiated protection. Dynamic media ranges and NAT complicate firewall policy; use the actual deployed ranges and peers, not the broad historical port lists in a book.

Historical references to SSLv3, TLSv1, old phone defaults, and vendor products are architectural context, not current configuration recommendations. Use currently supported vendor security profiles and organizational cryptographic policy; do not assume all modern SIP or IAX deployments share the books' defaults.
verify: Obtain a diagram of signaling/media/management flows with endpoint and proxy owners, allowed source networks, actual port ranges, certificate trust policy, and recording integrations.

Review authentication/authorization requirements for endpoint registration, call setup, management, and deregistration from configuration or existing test evidence. Do not issue unsolicited registrations or disconnect requests.

With consenting test endpoints place one normal synthetic call. Collect redacted endpoint/proxy session diagnostics showing negotiated signaling security, media protection, peer identity validation, and each traversed hop; do not record real conversation audio or key material.
Compare firewall/SBC rules with required peers and negotiated media ranges. Use existing approved connection evidence or tightly bounded service-discovery checks; UDP silence is not proof of closure.
Inspect whether endpoints require protected modes or silently allow unprotected fallback. Validate supplier-supported policy and logs; do not force a downgrade or replay media.

branches.condition: Signaling is protected but media is unencrypted
branches.outcome: Report media confidentiality exposure from the relevant network vantage; signaling TLS is not the remedy for media.

branches.condition: One proxy leg lacks protection or peer validation
branches.outcome: Report the specific hop and trust gap, not end-to-end security.

branches.condition: Only a nominal secure port or SRTP-looking capture is available
branches.outcome: Protection remains unverified until negotiated session and configuration evidence agree.

fix: Require current vendor-supported signaling security with peer/certificate validation on each required hop and appropriate authenticated media protection and key management.
Restrict management and signaling to intended peers; use reviewed SBC/firewall policies and the smallest supported media ranges. Segmentation alone does not encrypt voice.
Disable inappropriate cleartext fallback where supported and test interoperability, recording requirements, and emergency-call functionality through approved procedures.
retest: Repeat a consented synthetic call and confirm negotiated protection on every required leg and normal audio in both directions.
Reconcile access rules with allowed and denied sources and verify management isolation. Document gateways or endpoints that cannot meet policy rather than calling the whole deployment secure.
detection: Monitor unexpected endpoint registrations, management changes, failed peer validation, and unprotected-mode negotiations without logging keys or conversation contents.
Correlate call quality and SBC/firewall errors after policy changes; network-security changes must not silently break availability.

provenance.reason: Explains signaling TLS and certificate validation; obsolete protocol versions are explicitly not adopted.
States that TLS-protected signaling with cleartext RTP still exposes audio and distinguishes SRTP.
Notes that SRTP looks similar on the wire and distinguishes confidentiality from integrity.
Explains dynamic media port and NAT/firewall difficulties; historical broad ranges are not copied.
Audit questions distinguish session controls, directory protection, and media encryption.

title: Validate the evidence-to-response chain with benign events
scope: Coordinated defensive logging checks and tabletop response exercises. Synthetic events only; no malicious execution, credential attacks, stealth, or detection bypass.
concepts: A recorded event, a collected event, an alert, and an acted-on incident are different milestones. Test the entire chain with a known harmless action and timestamp. An empty dashboard can mean no activity, disabled auditing, ingestion loss, wrong time range, or a broken query; it does not establish safety.

Useful evidence includes time/timezone, asset identity, actor or role, action, result, request/correlation ID, collector receipt, alert routing, and responder acknowledgment. Logs must not expose passwords, tokens, keys, sensitive documents, or unrestricted script contents. Protect their integrity, access, and retention while keeping enough detail to support diagnosis.

Response readiness includes preparation, detection/analysis, containment/recovery, and learning. Turn those phases into assigned actions and communications for the local organization. Book-era framework revision names and logging defaults are historical context; use current supported platform guidance and an organization-approved response process.

discover.title: Inspect recent PowerShell operational events
discover.code:
# Authorized Windows read access; operational log may be disabled or inaccessible.
# Does not enable logging or execute scripts. Avoid exporting message bodies containing secrets.
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational'; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1)} -MaxEvents 20 | Select-Object TimeCreated,Id,ProviderName
discover.interpretation: Output confirms local events exist in this log/time window, not that central collection or alerting works. Access errors, disabled channels, no events, and retention loss need separate diagnosis. Event identifiers and enabled logging features depend on platform and configuration.

verify: Choose one benign action already allowed by another guide, such as a synthetic denied object read or approved configuration read. Agree expected event fields and whether an alert is intended; notify responders and label the exercise.
Record UTC action time, test principal, asset, and correlation ID. Compare source logs with collector receipt and detection query results; measure delay at each stage and check clock alignment.
If an expected event is absent, check logging policy, channel health, agent permissions, forwarding, retention, query filters, and time window. Distinguish telemetry missing from rule not matching.
For an intended test alert verify ticket/on-call delivery and acknowledgment against the agreed service level. Do not create real harmful behavior merely to stimulate an alert.

Run a tabletop using only a stated hypothetical incident: identify who analyzes, authorizes containment, preserves evidence, communicates, restores service, and records lessons. Gather actual contact/approval evidence without disabling production systems.

branches.condition: Source event exists but collector lacks it
branches.outcome: Treat forwarding/ingestion as the gap; rule tuning will not fix absent telemetry.

branches.condition: Collector has event but intended alert or acknowledgment fails
branches.outcome: Investigate query, routing, and response ownership separately and retain timing evidence.

branches.condition: No alert was intended for the benign event
branches.outcome: Use it to assess collection only; do not count silence as a detection failure.

branches.condition: Logs expose secrets or sensitive content
branches.outcome: Restrict access immediately through approved handling, assess disclosure, and correct logging without destroying needed evidence.

fix: Enable supported audit sources needed for the threat model and repair collection with health monitoring and synchronized time.
Define detection ownership, triage criteria, escalation contacts, and approved containment decisions; minimize sensitive fields and protect retained evidence.
Translate tabletop gaps into assigned playbook changes and due dates; use current supported logging features rather than assuming historical defaults.
retest: Repeat the same benign labeled event and compare event completeness, ingestion delay, intended alert routing, and acknowledgment.

Re-run the failed tabletop decision or communication step with responsible staff and document improvement and remaining gaps. Successful telemetry does not establish coverage of all attacker behavior.
detection: Monitor collector heartbeats, ingestion lag, volume discontinuities, audit-policy changes, and on-call delivery failures.
Review closed incidents and benign exercise results for missing evidence and update playbooks. Keep synthetic-event identifiers so routine assessments are not mistaken for real incidents.

provenance.reason: Describes a mature IR program as the foundation for coordinated exercises and improvement in detection/response time.
Lists response phases and the need for role-specific playbooks, workflow, communications, and lessons learned.
Explains that logging a PowerShell launch alone is insufficient and that richer module logging has limits; used only for visibility assessment.
